title: The Ptarmigan That Hid a Village
creature: A ptarmigan who hides what the storm is looking for
summary: For two days in 1953 the pass could not find the houses, and the houses were perfectly fine.

chapters.title: The Bird That Is Not There
chapters.text: A ptarmigan in winter is white, and this is the least interesting thing about a ptarmigan. Isla's great-grandmother had made this point to her at least thirteen times, always in the same slightly irritated tone, as though somebody had just that moment suggested otherwise. Lots of things are white in the snow. The hare goes white. The stoat goes white. Being white is easy and it does not work very well, because snow is not one colour and a white thing on it casts a shadow and has an edge. Isla had been made to prove this to herself at about eight, on the slope behind the house, with a white plastic bag and a good deal of complaining. Her great-grandmother had put the bag in the snow forty metres off and told her to find it, and Isla had found it in under two seconds and had said so, at some volume. "Aye," the old woman had said. "That's white. Now find the bird." What the ptarmigan does is different, and Isla did not properly understand it until she was eleven and had spent forty minutes on the ridge above Cnoc Dubh looking directly at a bird she had been told was four metres away. They do not hide themselves. They hide. They sit in a scoop in the lee of a stone, where the light is already flat, and they do not move at all, and the not-moving is not stillness — it is a positive act, sustained, for hours. Everything about the animal is arranged to remove the two things an eye is actually looking for, which are the outline and the change. The feathers go right down over the feet so there are no legs to make a line. The black tail is tucked. The eye, which is the one thing that cannot be white, is held behind the rock. And when you do finally see one, you cannot then un-see it, and you sit there feeling foolish, and seventeen metres away there is another one you also cannot see. The moment of seeing is the strangest part and it does not get less strange with practice. There is nothing there, and there is nothing there, and there is nothing there — and then there is a bird, entire, obvious, four metres away, in a place your eye has crossed perhaps two hundred times in the last half hour. Nothing has changed. The bird did not move; that is precisely what it has been not doing. What changed is on your side, and it happens all at once, and it cannot be undone: once you have seen that bird you will see it every time you look at it for the rest of the afternoon. Which means, and Isla worked this out on the ridge at eleven with her hands going numb, that the entire trick is being run against something in your head rather than against your eyes. "That," said her great-grandmother, "is the whole business. It is not about looking like snow. It is about not being findable." She was ninety-four that year. She had been eleven herself in 1953.

chapters.title: The Second of February
chapters.text: Isla had heard the story of the storm since she was small and had heard it the way you hear a family story, which is to say in fragments, out of order, with the ending known before the beginning. She got it properly in one go, on a wet afternoon in October, with a recorder on the table, because her school had set a local history project and Isla had realised on the bus that she was sitting on the best one in the county. Her great-grandmother talked for fifty-one minutes and Isla did not interrupt once. The storm came in on the second of February 1953 and it was, in that part of the country, the worst in a hundred years. It is in the books. There were people killed in it on the east coast and there was a ferry lost and the number is in every account of that winter. At Cnoc Dubh there were fourteen houses in a hollow under the ridge, with a road in from the pass and nothing else. Fourteen houses, sixty-one people, one telephone in the schoolroom that had gone with the line on the second night, and enough coal and meal in every house to sit out a fortnight without anybody thinking about it twice, because that was simply how you lived there in February. That is the detail that people always miss, her great-grandmother said, and it is the one that matters most. Nobody in that hollow was in trouble. They were not running short and they were not frightened and they were not waiting to be found. They were snowed in, in the ordinary way, in a place where being snowed in was a thing that happened most years and was chiefly a nuisance about the milk. The road went on the first night. That was normal; the road went most winters. What was not normal was the second night, when the power line came down, and the third day, when the drifts across the mouth of the hollow were high enough that a man could walk over the top of a telegraph pole and one of them did, on purpose, to say he had. By the fourth day the county had decided that Cnoc Dubh was a problem. They sent a party from Ardmore, over the pass, thirteen men on foot with poles. This is in the county record and Isla has since read the record, which is one paragraph long and extremely dry. The party went over the pass on the morning of the fifth. They came back to Ardmore that evening and reported that they had been unable to reach the settlement. Isla found the actual wording in the county archive in Inverness, which took her two letters and a train. *Party unable to reach Cnoc Dubh owing to conditions. Returned 1740.* That is it. Thirteen men, a full day on the hill in February, and one line. She sat in the reading room and looked at it for a while and understood something about records that has stayed with her, which is that the paper is not the event; the paper is what somebody had the energy to write down at the end of a very long day. They went again on the sixth, in better weather, with a local man who had been born in the hollow. They came back and reported the same. On the seventh an aircraft went over. That is also in the record. It flew the length of the glen at low level in clear conditions and reported no sign of the houses and no smoke. And in the hollow, on the fifth, and the sixth, and the seventh, fourteen houses had their fires lit and their chimneys going and thirteen children were being made to do lessons at kitchen tables, and nobody in Cnoc Dubh had the faintest idea that anybody was looking for them.

chapters.title: The Argument
chapters.text: Isla's history teacher liked the project very much and had one objection, which was reasonable, and which Isla had already thought of on the bus home. Drifting. Whiteout. A hollow under a ridge fills, the geography changes shape, and a party on foot in a hundred-year storm walks past the mouth of a glen they think they know. It happens. It has happened many times, it is in mountain rescue literature, and there is nothing whatever mysterious about it. The aircraft was harder but not impossible. Low cloud on the seventh, said the teacher. Wrong glen. Smoke does not rise in that kind of cold; it lies down in the hollow and looks like more snow. Isla wrote all of that in the project, fairly, in its own section, because her great-grandmother had told her to. That was the thing that surprised her most about the whole business. She had expected the old woman to defend it. Instead, when Isla brought the objections back and put them on the table like an accusation, her great-grandmother listened to all of them and said: "Aye. That'll be it, likely." Isla had come in ready for an argument and had a page of notes, and found herself entirely without a use for either. "You don't believe that." "I didn't say I believed it. I said it'll be it." She was doing something with her hands that she had done for eighty years. "There's a difference between what happened and what you can say happened, and you're eleven, and it's about time you learnt which one goes in a school project." Then she said the other thing, which is the reason Isla has never stopped thinking about any of it. She said that on the fifth of February 1953, at first light, she had gone out to the peat stack, and there had been a ptarmigan sitting in the scoop on the top of the ridge directly above the hollow. That it had been there on the sixth. That it had been there on the seventh, and that her father had seen it too, and that her father — who was not a fanciful man, who kept accounts, who had no patience with any of this — had stood in the yard looking up at the ridge with a bucket in his hand for a long time and had then come in and said nothing at all. And that on the morning of the eighth it was gone, and by eleven o'clock the party from Ardmore came over the top and down into the hollow without any difficulty whatsoever. Isla asked the obvious question, which was whether her great-grandmother thought the bird had done it. The answer took a while. "I think there was a bird on that ridge for three days and I think on the fourth day there wasn't, and I think thirteen men walked into this glen on the fourth day who couldn't find it on the second." She looked at Isla. "That's what I know. Everything past that is what I'd be making up, and I'm ninety-four, and I've watched a lot of people make things up about that week, and I've never once done it and I'm not starting now."

chapters.title: The Ridge in December
chapters.text: Isla is fifteen now and Cnoc Dubh has six houses in it and a tarmac road that is cleared by a machine from Ardmore, usually within a day. Her great-grandmother died in the March after the project. The storm came on the eleventh of December and it was not a 1953 storm and nobody has pretended otherwise. It was a bad one. The road went, the power went for nine hours, and the school in Ardmore was shut for three days, and the whole thing was on the regional news for about ninety seconds. Isla went out on the second morning to see to the hens. It was flat white and there was no wind at all, which is the thing that happens after, and the ridge above the hollow was a clean grey line against a sky the colour of a plate. She stood in the yard with the feed bucket and looked up at the scoop. She looked for a long time — long enough that her hands went, long enough that her mother came to the door and asked her what on earth she was doing — and she did not see anything at all, and she went in. She has thought about this a great deal. If it was there, she could not have seen it. That is not a get-out; that is the entire, well-documented, un-mysterious biology of the animal. Isla has sat four metres from a ptarmigan on a bare ridge in daylight and been unable to find it while being told exactly where to look. So the honest position, and the one she has settled on, is that she does not know whether there was a bird on the ridge above her house on the twelfth of December, and that there is no available method by which she could have found out, and that this is not a failure of the investigation. It is what the animal is. What she does know is that the machine from Ardmore came on the fourteenth and that everybody was fine. She goes out and looks anyway, every time, and she is aware that this is not evidence of anything. Her mother thinks it is a habit picked up from an old woman and is gently amused by it, and Isla lets her think that, because the alternative is a conversation she does not want to have on a doorstep in the cold. She has been up to the scoop once in summer, in July, when they are brown and much easier. There is a hollow in the peat up there about the size of a dinner plate, in the lee of a stone, worn smooth, facing directly down the glen at the fourteen — now six — chimneys of Cnoc Dubh. She did not measure it. She sat beside it for a while and then went down.
